summary: Retain both inherited glosses and the Russian editorial question. Active Preterit is newly evidenced by papers and Joseph. Active mṣakril-e differs from Detransitive mṣakri-lan: l-series agents versus affected possessors must be distinguished.

Detransitive Preterit describes becoming absent and a durative missing state (Joseph forty years); Infectum describes prospective, conditional and narrative disappearance. The forms do not force an eventive reading.
Part. Pass. is supported by mṣákro-yo and masculine mṣakro after fāš. The reader's Preterit filing for Uso is corrected in decisions only. No existing example is moved.

Lookup found no skr entry; ṣkr 1 is intoxication and sxr is closing, with different forms. The inherited under-skr instruction has no retrievable target, but its historical editorial intent cannot be reconstructed here. Keep ṣkr 2 and spellings msakri/mṣakri without normalization.
No new idiomatic phrase is warranted. The following azzé me kise idiom in the Uso account is a separate verb and does not establish a new ṣkr idiom.
94/52 has partial alignment. Its supplied German is not quoted in any addition.
Jan Beṯ-Şawoce: the supplied English is project machine translation. All semantic decisions rest on the Turoyo; English quotations are retained verbatim and are not edition translations.

Language disappearance and human disappearance in the Sayfo retain the Detransitive loss sense. The explicit contrast mṣakri aw qṭili distinguishes being missing from being killed; disappearance must not be glossed as death.

The quoted title in Jan 4.I/96 is disambiguated by 4.I/307: Aṯra is a female personal name. The supplied English land interpretation is rejected in analysis, without rewriting that source translation.
Plural mṣakre after latne is treated as Part. Pass.; finite feminine mṣakro remains in Detransitive Preterit, parallel to the inherited witch example. Round 1 already establishes the participial box.
The inherited under skr cross-reference and spelling irregularities are preserved; the present evidence does not identify their editorial target. No new idiom or sense is warranted.
